Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests Introduction This section is provided to familiarize the service technician with acceptable procedures for the testing and evaluation of various problems that could be encountered on standby generators with liquid-cooled engines. Use this section of the manual in conjunction with Section 3.3 DC Troubleshooting Flowcharts. The numbered tests in this section correspond with those flowcharts. Most tests can be performed with a digital multimeter (DMM). An AC frequency meter is required, where frequency readings must be taken. A clamp-on ammeter may be used to measure AC loads on the generator. NOTE: Refer to specific engine service manuals for engine adjustment and maintenance procedures. Testing and troubleshooting methods covered in this section are not exhaustive. No attempt has been made to discuss, evaluate and advise the standby service trade of all conceivable ways in which service and trouble diagnosis must be performed. Accordingly, anyone who uses a test method not recommended herein must first satisfy himself that the procedure or method he has selected will jeopardize neither his nor the products safety. Safety Service personnel who work on this equipment must be made aware of the dangers of such equipment. Extremely high and dangerous voltages are present that can kill or cause serious injury. Gaseous fuels are highly explosive and can be ignited by the slightest spark. Engine exhaust gases contain deadly carbon monoxide gas that can cause unconsciousness or even death. Contact with moving parts can cause serious injury. When working on this equipment, use common sense and remain alert at all times. Never work on this equipment while physically or mentally fatigued. If a component, device, or system is not understood, do not work on it. Test 35 – Check 7.5 Amp Fuse General Theory The 7.5 amp fuse is located on the generator control console. A blown fuse will prevent battery power from reaching the circuit board with the same result as setting the controller to OFF. The display and menus will remain active, but the unit will not be able to crank, and the controller might reset. Procedure 1. Remove and inspect the 7.5 amp fuse (F1). Visually inspect the fuse and fuse element. If the fuse element looks good, or if it cannot be visually inspected, test the fuse for an open with a DMM or Continuity Tester. Results 1. If the fuse if good, refer back to the Flow Chart. 2. If the fuse is bad, it should be replaced. Use only an identical 7.5 amp replacement fuse. 3. If fuse continues to blow, proceed to Problem 33 Flow Chart. Test 36–Check Fuses General Theory An in-line fuse is a circuit-breaking safety device that protects electrical devices from overcurrent. Overcurrent damages components and causes excessive heat and fire hazards. IMPORTANT NOTE: It is rarely acceptable to simply replace a fuse. Open (blown) fuses are more of a symptom and less of a cause when diagnosing a problem. Typically some underlaying issue caused the fuse to “blow,” such as a short-to-ground or short-topower, or a defective component that draws more than the rated amps. Fuses occasionally will “blow” due to heat and vibration. Procedure 1. Refer to the appropriate wiring diagram to locate 15 or 25 Amp fuse(s) in line with the DC alternator (Wires 13 and Wire 15 if equipped) 2. Locate and inspect condition of the 15 or 25 amp fuse (if equipped). Results 1. Replace any faulty fuses as needed and retest. 2. If all fuses are good, refer back to the flow chart. Test 39 – Test AUTO-OFF-MANUAL Switch Procedure 1. Access the dealer menu by using the dealer password. 2. Navigate to SUB MENUS and press ENTER. Navigate to DEALER and press ENTER. Navigate to TEST and press ENTER. The first screen shown will be “INPUTS”. Diagnostic Repair Manual 119

56A 0 56A 0 Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 3. With the inputs screen displayed, press and hold the AUTO button. Observe input 9 on the controller display. Input 9 will change from “0” to “1” momentarily. Release the AUTO button. NOTE: If Utility voltage is not available, unit will crank. 4. With the inputs screen displayed, press and hold the MANUAL button. Observe input 10 on the controller display. Input 10 will change from “0” to “1”. Release the MANUAL button. NOTE: Unit will crank and run. 5. With the inputs screen displayed, press and hold the OFF button. Observe input 8 on the controller display. Input 8 will change from “0” to “1”. Release the OFF button. Results 1. If controller failed either Step 3, 4 or 5, replace the controller assembly. 2. If the controller passed Step 3, 4 or 5, continue on the good test path on the flow chart. Test 40 – Check Wire 56 General Theory During an automatic start or when starting manually, an internal crank relay energizes. Each time the crank relay energizes, the controller delivers 12 VDC to a start contactor (SC) and the engine cranks. This test will verify (a) that the crank relay in the controller is energizing, and (b) that the controller is delivering 12 VDC to the SC. NOTE: Wire 56 becomes Wire 56A if equipped with an e-Stop switch. SPLICE 4 13 SC LOCATED BACK OF CUSTOMER CONNECTION BOX 16 SM 0 GND 56A J2-22 Figure 3-47. Starter Contactor 003100a Procedure 1. Navigate to the appropriate OUTPUTS screen. 2. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL and observe digital output number 6. If the controller is working correctly, output number 6 will change from 0 to 1. Observe and record the change in state. a. If the display changed from 0 to 1 proceed to Step 3. b. If the display did not change, replace controller. 3. Locate the starter contactor (SC) on the bulkhead in the engine compartment. 4. Disconnect Wire 56 from the SC. 5. Set a DMM to measure DC voltage. 120 6. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 56 and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. 7. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. Measure and record the DC voltage indicated a. If the DMM indicated battery voltage, discontinue testing and refer to the flow chart. b. If the DMM did not indicate battery voltage, proceed to Step 8. 8. Using the correct back probe connectors, connect one meter test lead to Wire 56 at the J connector on the Evolution controller and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. 9. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. Measure and record the DC voltage indicated. a. If the DMM indicated battery voltage, discontinue testing and proceed to Step 10. b. If the DMM did not indicate battery voltage, retest. If the DMM did not indicate battery voltage, replace controller. 10. Disconnect the appropriate connector from the back of the controller. 11. Set the DMM to measure resistance. 12. Connect one meter test lead to the Wire 56 pin location and the other meter test lead to the disconnected Wire 56 at the SC. Measure and record the resistance indicated. a. If the DMM indicated CONTINUITY, inspect connections at the controller connector. b. If the DMM indicated INFINITY, repair or replace wire between the controller connector and the SC. Results If repairs and/or tests are good, refer to the flow chart. Test 41 – Check Voltages at Starter Contactor General Theory The starter contactor (SC) is used to apply battery voltage to the starter solenoid allowing the starter motor to turn the engine over during cranking operations. The controller applies battery voltage to Wire 56 on the starter contactor relay (SC). When Wire 56 has battery voltage applied to the SC, the battery voltage from Wire 13 is permitted through the SC and to Wire 16 that goes to the starter solenoid. SPLICE 4 13 SC LOCATED BACK OF CUSTOMER CONNECTION BOX 16 SM 0 GND 56A J2-22 Figure 3-48. Starter Contactor 003100a Diagnostic Repair Manual

NOTE: Wire 56 becomes Wire 56A if equipped with an e-Stop switch. Procedure 1. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 13 at the starter contactor and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. Battery voltage should always be present. a. If battery voltage is present, proceed to Step 2. b. If little or no battery voltage is present, verify that Wire 13 is not pinched, cut, or is open or has high resistance. 2. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 16 at the starter contactor and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. 3. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. Measure and record the voltage indicated by the meter. Results 1. If battery voltage is present at Wires 13 and 16, refer to the flow chart. 2. If little or no battery voltage is present on Wire 16 and Wires 56 and 13 have battery voltage present, replace the starter contactor relay (SCR). Test 42 – Check Battery Voltage at Starter Motor (SM) Procedure 1. Set the DMM to measure DC voltage. 2. Place the negative (-) test lead to a clean frame ground and the positive (+) test lead to Wire 16 on the starter solenoid. 3. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. Results 1. If battery voltage is present when setting the AUTOOFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL, and the engine still didn’t turn over, replace the starter motor. 2. If battery voltage is present when setting the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL, and the starter motor tried to engage (pinion engaged), but engine did NOT crank, check for mechanical binding of the engine or rotor. 3. If there is little or no battery voltage present, verify Wire 16 is not pinched or cut and inspect for any other conditions that would not allow battery voltage to Wire 16. Test 45 – Check Battery and Cables General Theory Battery power is used to (a) crank the engine and (b) to power the circuit board. Low or no battery voltage can result in the failure of the engine to crank and the controller to blank out and restart in either MANUAL or Diagnostic Repair Manual Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests AUTO modes of operation. Also, if there is a loose connection or corrosion associated with a wire (positive or negative), battery voltage may be present, but because of high resistance, will not allow current to flow. Electrical voltage drop varies according to current flow. Unless the circuit is operated so current flows through it, the voltage drop cannot be measured. To properly measure voltage drop, a crank attempt must be performed. This test will determine whether the battery, battery cables, or both are at fault. NOTE: The battery charger in the control panel is not designed to recharge a dead battery. Procedure A. Inspect Battery Cables, Terminals, and Connections 1. Inspect battery cables and battery posts. 2. If cable clamps or terminals are corroded, clean away all corrosion. NOTE: If corrosion cannot be cleaned or eliminated, replace the component in question. 3. Verify all cable clamps are tight. The Red Battery cable from the starter contactor (SC) must be securely attached to the positive (+) battery post. The Black cable from the frame ground stud must be tightly attached to the negative (-) battery post. 4. If the above inspection points have been verified satisfactory, proceed to Procedure B. Procedure B. Perform a Battery Open Circuit Voltage Test 1. Remove the T1 fuse from the transfer switch or disconnect the BCH with Wires J11 and J12 connector for T1 (A) to disable the battery charger. 2. Set a DMM to measure DC voltage. 3. Connect the red meter test lead to the positive battery post and connect the black meter test lead to the negative battery post. 4. Measure and record the OCV (Open Circuit Voltage) a. If battery voltage is below 12.1 VDC, but greater than 9.0 VDC, or if the engine does not crank (turn over), proceed to Procedure C. b. If battery voltage is 12.2 VDC or above and the engine does crank, proceed to Procedure D. Procedure C. Perform a Conductance Test with a Conductance Type Battery Tester IMPORTANT NOTE: To properly load test a battery when using a resistance-type load tester, the battery must be completely full of electrolytes, fully charged and the load applied must be 1/2 of the battery's CCA Rating. (e.g. 540/2=270A) For this reason, a resistance-type load tester is not recommended. 121

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 1. Remove the 7.5 amp fuse from the controller. 2. Test results should not indicate anything lower than 60% of the battery's rated CCA. If battery CCA is 60% or less, replace the battery with new. 4. The generator will not crank and start on occurrence of a utility power outage unless in AUTO mode. In addition, the generator will not exercise as programmed unless in AUTO mode. Turn ON the utility power supply to the transfer switch after the generator starts up and transfers to the standby source. Transfer to the utility source will occur. Generator shutdown will occur after an engine cool down timer has timed out. Results 1. If normal automatic operation is obtained, discontinue tests. 2. If the engine does not crank when utility power is turned off, proceed to Problem 15 – Unit Will Not Crank When AUTO-OFF-MANUAL Mode is Set to MANUAL. 3. If engine cranks but won’t start, proceed to Problem 18 – Unit Cranks But Will Not Start (Overcrank Alarm). 4. If the engine cranks and starts, but transfer to standby does NOT occur, refer to the appropriate transfer switch diagnostic manual. Diagnostic Repair Manual

5. If transfer to standby occurs, but transfer to utility does NOT occur when utility source voltage is restored, proceed to Test 49 – Check Utility Sensing. Test 48 – Check Maintenance Disconnect Switch General Theory In a 2-wire start configured transfer switch, a maintenance disconnect switch is installed in the switch to disable its automatic features to prevent a generator from starting and a transfer occurring while a technician is working on a piece of equipment. Procedure 1. Locate the maintenance disconnect switch inside the transfer switch. 2. Verify that it is in the AUTO position. Results 1. If the switch was in the AUTO position, refer to the flow chart. 2. If the switch was OFF, place in AUTO position and try a simulated power outage. Test 49 – Check Utility Sensing General Theory The Evolution Controller will utilize N1 and N2 to monitor incoming utility voltage. This voltage can be viewed in the Dealer Menu, Test, and Inputs screen. The Evolution controller will sense the loss of utility voltage and will start the generator. Procedure 1. Enter the Dealer Password, Navigate to the Sub Menus screen, Dealer screen, Test screen, and to the Inputs screen. 2. Record the voltage indicated on the display. NOTE: Check the “Util Volts Low” setting programmed int the controller under the Dealer Edit screen. Make note of this setting. 3. Set the DMM to measure AC voltage. 4. Locate the TB2 terminal strip in the customer connection box. 5. Connect one meter test lead to terminal 1 (Wire N1) and the other meter test lead to terminal 2 (Wire N2). Measure and record the voltage indicated. Results 1. If the voltage observed in Step 2 is below the “Util Volts Low” programmed setting and the generator is not starting in AUTO mode, replace the controller Diagnostic Repair Manual Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 2. If the voltage observed in Step 2 was not correct and the correct utility voltage was measured in step 5, repair or replace the wiring between TB2 and the J1 connector. 3. If the DMM did not indicate proper voltage in Step 5, use the appropriate Transfer Switch Diagnostic Manual for testing the Utility Sensing circuit to the TB2 block. AC Customer Connections Test 51 – Verify 2-Wire or 3-Wire Start Enabled General Theory Start Sequence: 1. Transfer switch sends start command: • It closes contact between 183 (N/O) and 178 (COM). • This pulls Wire 183 low (close to 0 VDC). • Generator controller detects this low signal while in AUTO mode. • Generator starts: crank → fire → run. Stop Sequence: 1. Transfer switch sends stop command: • It opens the contact between 183 and 178. • If a cooldown is programmed, generator enters cooldown. • Generator shuts down after cooldown. Note on Voltage Logic: • When the wire is “pulled low”, it typically means it's at 0 VDC or ground, compared to the system's logic high (12 VDC). • The generator controller must be designed to interpret this correctly. Procedure 1. Set AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to AUTO. a. AUTO mode allows the system to operate based on automated controls or external signals. 2. Place a Jumper Wire Across Terminal TB3-3 and TB3-4 123

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests a. Go to Terminal Block 3 (TB3) - this is located in the customer connection area. • TB3 terminal 3: connected to Wire 183 • TB3 terminal 4: connected to Wire 178. b. Verify the wire is secure and connections are tight. c. If generator starts, the problem is in the transfer switch. d. If no start, continue to Step 3. 3. Locate TB2 Terminal Block. • Go to the customer connection box. • Identify the TB2 terminal block. 4. Disconnect the customer-supplied 2-wire start wire • Locate the 2-wire start wire connected by the customer to TB2. • Carefully disconnect both wires from the termi- nal block. • Label them if needed for easy reconnection. • Verify they are not touching anything metal or each other after removal. 5. Set a DMM to Measure DC Voltage 6. Measure Voltage Between Wire 183 and Wire 178. a. If DMM indicates 5 VDC, replace the Evolution controller. If the DMM indicates 0 VDC, continue to Step 7. 7. Set a DMM to measure continuity. a. Place one meter lead on Wire 178 at the Controllers J1 connector and place the other meter lead on TB3 pin 4, Wire 178. b. If continuity is measured, continue to Step 8. c. If continuity is not measured, repair Wire 178 from the Controller to the TB connector. 8. Set a DMM to measure continuity. a. Place one meter lead on Wire 183 at the Controllers J1 connector and place the other meter lead on TB3 pin 3, Wire 183. b. If continuity is not measured, repair Wire 183 from the Controller to the TB connector. c. If continuity is measured, retest starting with Procedure #1. Test 52 – Check Fuel System (Diesel Units) General Theory – Fuel Flow Process 1. Fuel Priming Pump: a. Function: Draws fuel from the tank. b. May have a sediment/water trap installed before it to catch contaminants. 2. Fuel Filter: a. Function: Cleans the fuel before it reaches the injection pump. b. Also serves as a water separator and includes a drain valve for removing water. 124 3. Fuel Injection Pump: a. Function: Sends fuel under high pressure to the injectors. b. Requires fuel for lubrication. Air in the system can damage it, so it must be primed before starting. 4. Fuel Injectors: a. Function: Spray fuel into a pre-combustion chamber (not directly into the cylinder). b. Injection occurs in two phases at different angles. c. Most fuel is injected when the injector valve is fully open. General Theory – Fuel Return System 1. Excess fuel and air are returned to the tank via the fuel return line. 2. Benefits: a. Cools the injectors. b. Removes trapped air from the system.. Procedure A – Fuel System Prime 1. Loosen the air bleed screw and work priming pump until bubbles are observed. Place a shop rag near the air bleed screw to catch any loss of fuel. When all bubbles are purged and replaced by a solid stream of fuel, depress pump handle and tighten the air bleed screw. 2. Loosen injection pump bleed screw. The bleed screw is normally located on the injection pump fuel return line. 3. Work priming pump until bubbles are observed. Tighten the bleed screw when all bubbles are purged. 4. Locate the highest injection line on the back of the injection pump. This line will usually coincide with the number 1 injector. 5. Loosen the corresponding injector line, at the injector. 6. Place unit in MANUAL. As the unit cranks, a foamy bubbly fuel spray should bleed from the loosened injection line. Once the foam has been replaced with a steady stream of fuel, place unit in OFF and tighten the injection line. NOTE: Unit may attempt to run while performing Step 6. NOTE: In extreme cases of an “air bound” injection system it may be necessary to loosen all the injection lines at the injectors to purge the air from the system. Procedure B – Sight Glass Test 1. Identify and remove the fuel supply line from the fuel filter to the inlet of the injection pump. 2. See Figure 3-51. Assemble a fuel line test tube by placing two 12 inch sections on the in-line ends of a tee fitting. Use clamps to prevent air leaks. Diagnostic Repair Manual

Figure 3-51. Fuel Line Test Tube 005421 3. Install the fuel line test tube from the fuel filter to the inlet of the injection pump. Use clamps to prevent air leaks. 4. Install the fuel filter restriction gauge on the open barb that is perpendicular to the two in-line barbs. 5. Hold the restriction gauge above the filter, and follow the fuel priming procedure as outlined in the owner/s manual. While priming, no fuel should be allowed into the gauge. 6. Start and run unit. It may be necessary to let the unit run for a short time to remove all air from lines. It may also be necessary to “roll out the bubble” in the line. 7. With the engine running and all air purged from the line, and a new clean filter should read approximately -2 to -4 inches of mercury restriction. The restriction should be tested at a no load and in a fully loaded condition. 8. If the gauge reads -10 inches of mercury restriction, replace fuel filter. 9. While performing the test, visually inspect the fuel flow from the filter to the pump. If more than an occasional bubble can be seen, or if there is foam in the line, air is getting into the fuel system. Inspect and repair or replace fuel system components until the leak is found and/or repaired. 10. If no issue is found, return to the flowchart. Test 53 – Injector Drop Out Test Procedure 1. With the engine running, place shop towels around the fuel fitting on the injector connection. Then “crack open” (loosen) the injection line to each cylinder—one at a time. NOTE: Diesel fuel will spray out of the loosened injector fuel fitting, the engine drops speed or the sound changes, that cylinder is functioning properly. 2. If cracking open the line for the cylinder does not make a difference, or the white or black exhaust smoke clears, then that cylinder is not running well. Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 3. This test can also help to identify an engine knock problem. If the noise goes away when the injection line is loosened, there could be a problem with the injector or the injection pump. Test 54 – Cylinder Leak-down Test General Theory A cylinder leak-down test is a more accurate test for compression. When performing a cylinder leak-down test, the cylinder being tested is placed at TDC on the compression stroke. A leak-down tester is used to put a controlled amount of air into the cylinder and the gauge will indicated how much air is leaking. Read the gauge to see if the air loss is at an acceptable level. If there is excessive air leakage, the test will also show where the problem is. • If air can be heard leaking from the intake manifold, then a leaking intake valve is likely. • Air leaking from the output of the exhaust system indicates a leaking exhaust valve. • Air bubbling in the radiator or around the cylinder head indicates a cracked head or a faulty head gasket. • Air leaking from the test cylinder to the cylinder next to it indicates possible faulty head gasket. NOTE: There will always be air leaking from the crankcase. If the gauge shows excessive leakage and the only place air can be heard is coming from the crankcase, then the piston rings/cylinder bore can be suspected. 005424 Figure 3-52. Test 55 – Turbo Charger Boost and CAC Leak Test General Theory If a unit will not pull full load, or emits excessive black smoke, a boost pressure test can determine if the turbo charger, engine air inlet piping or charge air cooler are leaking or not performing. Procedure – Turbo Charger Boost Pressure Test 1. With the engine not running, locate the test port on the intake manifold (this will typically be an NPT pipe plug). 2. Remove the plug and insert a pressure gauge (follow the directions of the test gauge being used). 3. Start the engine. Run unit at no load and load the unit to full load, or run the maximum load that can be achieved if full load can not be attained. 4. Record the boost pressure at 25%, 50%, 75% and full load. • If boost pressure is within acceptable parameters and black smoke still persists, then an injector may be the issue. • If boost pressure is low, check for a pressure leak in the air piping system or charge air cooler (if equipped). Procedure – Charge Air Cooler Leak Test NOTE: To prevent debris from entering the engine, cover the turbocharger exhaust and intake piping while the charge air cooler is disconnected. NOTE: Before performing the leakage test, visually inspect the core, tanks, and welds for cracks and holes. If the cooler fails this visual inspection, REPLACE the charge air cooler. NOTE: It is not necessary to remove the charge air cooler from the unit to perform this test. 126 1. Disconnect turbocharger piping from the charge air cooler. 2. Follow the charge air cooler tester directions to install the tester on the charge air cooler. 3. Connect a filtered air supply to the air valve on the gauge/regulator assembly. 4. Open the air valve slightly, then SLOWLY increase air pressure until the gauge reads 30 psi (206.8 kPa). If necessary, adjust the air regulator until the gauge reads 30 psi (206.8 kPa). 5. Close the air valve and monitor the gauge with a stopwatch for 15 seconds. Note any decrease in air pressure. 6. If the pressure drop is 5 psi (34.5 kPa) or less in 15 seconds, the charge air cooler passes. If the pressure drop is more than 5 psi (34.5 kPa) in 15 seconds, the charge air cooler fails. 7. Test 58 – Check Fuel System (Gaseous Units) General Theory The engine-generator set was factory tested and adjusted using the primary fuel source (natural gas or LP) as the fuel supply. • An adequate gas supply and sufficient fuel pressure must be available or the engine will not start or run properly. • Refer to the correct unit specifications sheet for the units required fuel pressure. Fuel pressure specifications will vary based on engine and fuel type. • The gaseous fuel system must be properly tested for leaks following installation and periodically thereafter. No leakage is permitted. Leakage testing methods must strictly comply with gas codes. Maximum allowed deviation of fuel pressure at no-load or full load is 1 in of water column. DANGER Explosion and fire. Fuel and vapors are extremely flammable and explosive. No leakage of fuel is permitted. Keep fire and spark away. Failure to do so will result in death or serious injury. (000192) Procedure A water manometer (inches of Water column) is to be used to measure fuel pressure. Fuel pressure is measured at the inlet side of the regulator (top port— where the low fuel pressure switch is located). The fuel pressure should be within the upper and lower limits as stated in the unit’s specification sheet. The fuel pressure can be checked using a fuel pressure tester kit or any fuel pressure tester that measures inches of water column. 1. Turn off fuel to primary regulator by whatever means are provided. 2. See Figure 3-60. Connect a manometer to the provided Pete's Port or to Test port B on the Demand Regulator. Figure 3-60. The fuel solenoid (FS1) is only used during cranking operations and is controlled by (+) voltage on Wire 56B. This is the cold start fuel solenoid. Procedure 1. Test 68 – Check Actuator and Mixer Function General Theory The Bosch throttle actuator is an electronically controlled throttle-valve. It will control the amount of fuel and air mixture allowed into the engine so the engine can maintain proper speed through the entire load range of the unit. It is comprised of a throttle valve with electric drive, and a feedback circuit for throttle position back to the controller. The governor actuator that is in the Evolution control panel will control the throttle. Terms • Throat—The path where air flows through the governor. • Throttle Plate—The butterfly valve in the throat of the governor. • Rest Position—Position of the throttle plate with no power to unit. (Throttle plate almost perpendicular to the direction of air flow) • Open Position—Throttle plate parallel to the direction of air flow. • Upper Mechanical Stop (UMS)—Internal mechanical stop to prevent over rotation of throttle plate in the opening direction. (Past the open position) • Lower Mechanical Stop (LMS)—Internal mechanical stop to prevent over rotation of throttle plate in the closing direction. (Past the rest position) • Feedback circuit—The circuit between pins 2, 3, and 6 on the governor. Test 77 – Test Low Coolant Level Sensor General Theory Coolant is used to cool the engine by dissipating heat away from the engine. The coolant is cooled by passing through the radiator. If the coolant is not filled to the proper level for cooling, the engine may become damaged from excess heat build up over a period. Procedure 1. Locate and disconnect the low coolant level sensor from the radiator. 2. Install a 1000 Ohm resistor between wires 573 and 573A on the engine side of the harness. 3. If the coolant level fault cleared, go to results. If the coolant level fault is still remaining, continue to the next step. 4. Set DMM to measure AC voltage. 5. Remove the resistor and plug in the sensor to the wiring harness. 6. Back probe the sensor while plugged into the harness. 7. Measure AC voltage across Wire 573 and 573A. Polarity does not matter. 8. Set DMM to measure AC frequency. 9. Back probe the sensor while plugged into the harness. 10. Measure AC frequency across Wire 573 and 573A. Polarity does not matter. Diagnostic Repair Manual

If AC frequency reads 14.5–15.5 Hz in Step 10, the controller and wiring are good. 4. If results 2 and 3 are not true, refer back to flowchart. Test 78 – Check Wires 573 and 573A General Theory If the coolant sensor passes Test 77, check Wires 573 and 573A going to the sensor from the control panel to determine if the wires have continuity or are shorted. Procedure 1. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 2. Locate and disconnect the appropriate connector from the back of the controller. NOTE: The J2 connector houses both Wires 573 and 573A. Reference the controller identification or schematic drawing for proper plug and pin locations. 3. Locate and disconnect the low coolant level sensor. 4. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 573A in the harness at the controller and the other meter test lead to Wire 573A located at the coolant sensor connector plug (engine harness side). Measure and record the resistance indicated by the DMM. 5. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 573 in the harness at the controller and the other meter test lead to Wire 573 located at the coolant sensor connector plug (engine harness side). Measure and record the resistance indicated by the DMM. 6. Connect one meter lead to connector on Wire 573 and the other lead to the connector on Wire 573A. Check for a short between the wires. Results 1. If the DMM indicated resistance in Steps 4 and 5, replace controller. 2. If the DMM indicated an open (OL), or high resistance in either Step 4 or 5, repair or replace wire as needed. Test 79 – Check Coolant Temperature at Thermal Adapter General Theory This test will determine whether the coolant is overheated. Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests Procedure NOTE: A device to measure temperature is required for this procedure. 1. See Figure 3-68. Measure the temperature of the lower coolant hose at the location shown. 2. Record the temperature. Figure 3-68. Lower Coolant Hose 003114a Results 1. If temperature is within the engine specification, continue to the next step in the flowchart Test 114 – Coolant Sensor Circuit. 2. If temperature is not with the engine specification, continue to the next step in the flowchart Test 81 – Verify Fan/Fan Drive Operation. Test 80 – Check Coolant Level General Theory The coolant is used to cool the engine by dissipating heat away from the engine. The coolant is then cooled by passing though the radiator. If the coolant is not filled to the proper level for cooling, the engine may become damaged from excess heat build up over a period of time. Procedure 1. Remove the black rain cap on top of the generator housing. WARNING Risk of burns. Contents under pressure. Do not remove the radiator pressure cap while engine is hot. Doing so could result in death or serious injury. (000322a) NOTE: Verify that pressure in cooling system has bled off by squeezing the upper hose while wearing a suitable glove. If it collapses easily the pressure has bled off and it is safe to remove the cap. 2. Remove the radiator cap from the top of the radiator. 3. Verify the coolant filled to the bottom of the filler neck. Diagnostic Repair Manual 135

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 4. Also check the radiator overflow tank for the proper level (printed on the side of the tank) for cold and hot levels. Use only approved coolant to adjust the level. Results 1. If coolant level is low, fill the radiator with coolant prescribed by owners manual. Check for leaks. Check oil for a milky color (this may be a sign of a leak internal to the engine). 2. If coolant level is normal, refer to the flow chart. NOTE: The age of the coolant may also effect how well it operates with the coolant level sensor. If the coolant becomes dirty, this can cause intermittent faults to occur. Test 81 – Verify Fan/Fan Drive Operation General Theory The fan will blows air across the radiator to remove heat from the coolant. If the belt is broken or the fan is not operating correctly overheating will occur. Procedure 1. Locate the fan mounted directly to the engine. 2. Set AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. 3. Verify fan and proper belt operation. Results 1. Repair or replace failed components as identified. 2. If operation is good, refer to the flow chart. Test 82 – Check Coolant Hoses General Theory If maintenance is not performed regularly, the radiator hoses can become cracked or dry rotted, and may even break down due to weather exposure. The hose clamps can also become loose, causing coolant leaks. Check the radiator hoses when troubleshooting coolant issues. Procedure 1. Locate and inspect the upper and lower radiator hoses. Results 1. If no problem is found with either the upper or lower hoses on the generator and the problem continues, replace the thermostat. 2. If the hose displays blockage, remove the blockage from the area that is being affected. 136 Test 83 – Test Oil Pressure Switch General Theory Proper oil pressure is vital to engine operation and longevity. The oil pressure switch is installed in the oil circuit of the engine to monitor oil pressure in the engine. If it indicates a low pressure situation it will trigger a shutdown and alarm in the controller. Procedure 1. Locate the low oil pressure sender. 2. Set a DMM to measure DC voltage. 3. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 86 at the low oil pressure sender and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. 0 VDC should be measured. 4. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. DANGER Automatic start-up. Disconnect normal power source and render unit inoperable before working on unit. Failure to do so will result in death or serious injury. (000236) 5. The DMM should read 0 VDC while cranking and approximately 5 VDC once the unit is at its rated speed and oil pressure is above 10 psi (69 kPa). Results 1. The measured voltage should start at 0 VDC, indicating the switch is closed. The voltage should climb to 5 VDC (non-ECM controlled) or 12 VDC (ECM controlled), indicating proper function of the switch. 2. If the voltage at the switch remained at 0 VDC, replace the switch. 3. If voltage at the switch exceeds 12 VDC on an ECM controlled engine, replace the ECM. If voltage exceeds 5 VDC at the switch on a nonECM controlled engine, replace the Evolution controller. Test 84 – Check Oil Level General Theory Correct level of clean oil is vital to engine performance and longevity. Periodic checking of the oil level and condition is necessary. Procedure Remove the oil dipstick and observe the oil level. Results 1. If oil level is low, reference the front of this manual for crankcase capacity and Owner's Manual for proper weight and type. Fill oil to proper level. 2. If oil level is too high, remove the excess oil from the engine. 3. If oil level is correct, refer to the flow chart. Diagnostic Repair Manual

Test 85 – Check Engine Oil Pressure General Theory If the engine can’t maintain a certain oil pressure range, engine damage may result due to improper lubrication. If the engine has too much oil pressure the engine may suffer severe internal and/or external damage during running operations. Tools Required • Oil pressure gauge Procedure 1. Remove the oil pressure switch from the engine block. 2. Insert oil pressure gauge. 3. Turn the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. IMPORTANT NOTE: The engine will crank and possibly start when the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch is set to MANUAL. NOTE: With the oil pressure switch removed, the engine will shut down for low oil pressure after 10 seconds. 4. Record the results. Results 1. If the unit doesn’t have oil pressure after 10 seconds, shut the unit down and reference the engine service manual. 2. If the oil pressure is within operating range between 35–90 psi (399–620 kPa), contact Technical Support. Test 86 – Check Wire 86 for Continuity or Short-to-Ground General Theory The Evolution controller on a non-ECM controlled engine or the ECM controller on an ECM controlled engine uses Wire 86 to monitor the low oil pressure switch. This monitors a possible problem with the engine internal oil pressure. If Wire 86 is shorted or pinched, the unit will shutdown after 10 seconds of running. Procedure 1. Turn the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to OFF. 2. Locate the low oil pressure switch and the appropriate connector located on the Evolution controller or ECM. 3. Disconnect Wire 86 from the low oil pressure switch. Disconnect the appropriate connector from the Evolution controller or ECM. (Refer to Appendix A Controller Identification for proper plug and pin location) 4. Set DMM to measure resistance. Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 5. Connect the positive test lead to Wire 86 on the harness oil pressure switch end and the negative test lead to the appropriate Wire 86 at the controller or ECM. Measure and record the resistance. 6. With Wire 86 still isolated from the Evolution controller or ECM, and the low oil pressure switch. Connect one meter test lead to disconnected Wire 86 and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. Measure and record the resistance. Results 1. If the DMM indicated open or high resistance in Step 5, repair or replace Wire 86 between the low oil pressure switch and controller connections. 2. If resistance (0.01–0.04 Ohms) is measured to the ground in Step 6, repair or replace Wire 86. 3. If resistance (0.01–0.04 Ohms) is measured in Step 5 and open in Step 6 refer to the flow chart. Test 88 – Test 120 Volt Input (T1) General Theory The controller requires 120 VAC supplied from the load side of the contactor in the transfer switch and a neutral to function properly. When the voltage on this circuit is supplied to the controller, it will allow the controller to remain on with battery voltage not present. The controller will be in a disabled state where the generator will not crank and or function properly. Procedure NOTE: An inspect battery alarm may appear while performing this test procedure. Ignore this alarm, it is a symptom of the test procedure. 1. Locate the 7.5 amp fuse on the controller. 2. Remove the fuse and observe the LCD screen. Results 1. If the controller remained illuminated or continued to show its status after the fuse was removed, the 120 VAC input is good. Refer to the flow chart. 2. If the controller powered down when the fuse was removed, the controller is not getting the 120 VAC input. Refer to the flow chart. Test 89 – Verify DC Voltage Output of the Controller General Theory The battery voltage of the unit can be viewed within the “Display” menu of the Evolution controller. This test procedure will verify battery voltage connections to the controller. Diagnostic Repair Manual 137

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests Procedure 1. Disable the 120 VAC battery charge circuit by removing the T1 fuse from the transfer switch or disconnecting the BCH connector from the control panel. 2. Navigate to the BATTERY VOLTAGE menu in the controller. a. Enter dealer password (ESC, UP, UP, DOWN, DOWN, ESC, ESC) b. Navigate to and select “Sub menu”. c. Navigate to and select “Dealer”. d. Navigate to and select “Display”. e. Navigate to “Battery Voltage”. 3. Record the displayed voltage. Results 1. If the battery voltage indicated on the display is greater than 12 VDC, the connections to the controller from the battery are good. Refer to the flow chart (Good). 2. If the battery voltage indicated on the display is 0 VDC, the connections to the controller are bad. Refer to the flow chart. 3. If the battery voltage indicated on the display is between 10–12 VDC, refer to the flow chart (Bad). Test 90 – Test DC Charge Current to the Battery General Theory Previous testing has verified the 120 VAC input connection and the battery connection. This test procedure will determine if there is a negative draw on the battery or a positive one, which will indicate successful operation of the charger. Procedure NOTE: An inspect battery alarm may be generated during this test procedure. It will not effect the results of the test and can be acknowledged when testing is complete. 1. Navigate to the charger status screen in the Dealer Display Menu using level 1 or 2 pass code. If the charger is OFF, set the generator to MANUAL mode and crank the engine for 2-3 seconds. 2. Disconnect the negative cable battery. 3. Set the DMM to measure DC amperage. NOTE: Consult the multimeter owner’s manual to verify proper setup of meter and that the internal fuse is good before proceeding. 4. Connect the positive (red) meter test lead to the negative battery post and connect the negative (black) meter test lead to disconnected negative battery cable. Measure and record the amperage. 138 Results 1. If the DMM indicated positive DC amperage between 50 milliamps to 2.5 amps, stop testing. The charger is functioning properly. 2. If the DMM indicated negative DC amperage, replace the controller. Figure 3-69. Positive DC Amps 002435 Figure 3-70. Negative DC Amps 002436 Test 91 – Check Wires 0 and 15 General Theory If the controller did not register voltage at the controller on the display or it was less then required, a possible cause could be a bad connection at the controller. Procedure 1. Disconnect the J1 connector from the back of the controller. 2. Set a DMM to measure DC voltage. 3. Connect one meter lead to J1-1 Wire 15 for a gaseous generator or Wire 13 for a diesel generator and the other meter lead to a clean ground. Measure the voltage. 4. Connect one meter lead to J1-2 Wire 15 for a gaseous generator or Wire 13 for a diesel generator and the other meter lead to a clean ground. Measure the voltage. 5. Connect one meter lead to J1-4 Wire 0 for all units and the other meter lead to the positive battery post. Measure the voltage. Results 1. If the DMM indicated battery voltage in Steps 3–5, replace controller. 2. If the DMM did not indicate battery voltage in any one of Steps 3–5, repair or replace respective wire as needed. 3. If approximately 0 VDC was not measured on Wire 0, repair or replace pin, connector, or Wire 0 as required. Diagnostic Repair Manual

Test 92 – Check T1 Voltage at Customer Connections and BCH Connector General Theory The T1 line for the battery charger located in the control panel is a 120 VAC fused circuit. The T1 line runs from the T1 lug of the transfer switch mechanism to the BCH connector on the control panel. If this voltage is not present Charger Missing AC will be displayed on the control panel. NOTE: Verify neutral is connected prior to performing this test. Procedure 1. Set a DMM to measure AC Voltage. 2. Connect one meter test lead to TB2 terminal 3 (Wire T1) at the customer connections in the generator. Connect the other meter test lead to TB2 terminal 4 (Wire NEU). If the DMM indicated 120 VAC, proceed to the next step. If the DMM did not indicate 120 VAC go to the results of this test. 3. Locate and disconnect the J11/J12 connector from the back of the controller. 4. Connect one-meter test lead to Wire T1 and the other meter test lead to the Neutral Wire. If 120 VAC was measured go to the results of this test. Results 1. If the DMM indicated less than 120 VAC or 0 in Step 2, refer to the flow chart. 2. If the DMM indicated less than 120 VAC in Step 4 Replace the control panel. Test 93 – Check T1 Voltage in Transfer Switch General Theory The T1 line for the battery charger located in the control panel is a 120 VAC fused circuit. The T1 line runs from the T1 lug of the transfer switch mechanism to the BCH connector on the control panel. If this voltage is not present Charger Missing AC will be displayed on the control panel. NOTE: Verify neutral is connected prior to performing this test. Procedure 1. Set the DMM to measure AC voltage. 2. Connect one meter test lead to the bottom side of the T1 fuse holder and the other meter test lead to the NEUTRAL connection. If 120 VAC is measured, go to next step. If 120 VAC was not measured, go to the results of this test. Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 3. Connect one meter test lead to the top side of the T1 fuse holder and connect the other test lead to the NEUTRAL connection. Measure and record the voltage. a. If the DMM indicated 120 VAC, proceed to Step 5. b. If the DMM indicated less than 120 VAC or 0, proceed to Step 4. 4. Verify that the utility MLCB is in the ON position. Measure voltage between the T1 lug and the neutral connection on the mechanism. 120 VAC should be measured. If 120 VAC was not measured, proceed to the results of this test. 5. On the generator panel, set the AUTO-OFF MANUAL switch to OFF. 6. Disconnect utility from the transfer switch. 7. See Figure 3-71. Remove fuse F3 from the fuse holder. N1A N2A T1A A A A F1 F2 F3 B B B N1 N2 T1 002633 Figure 3-71. Transfer Switch Fuse Block 8. Inspect and test fuses for an OPEN condition with a DMM set to measure resistance. CONTINUITY should be measured across the fuse. Results 1. If 120 VAC was not measured in Step 4, test the utility MLCB and replace as needed. 2. If continuity was not measured in Step 8, replace fuse and retest. 3. If 120 VAC was not measured in Step 2, refer to the flow chart. Test 97 – Check Flywheel/Crank Sensor General Theory The flywheel sensor (MPU1) is a dual purpose sensor. For engines that utilize internal ignition only, it is a crank sensor for ignition and an rpm sensor for governing. For units that use an external ignition system, it is only an rpm sensor. Diagnostic Repair Manual 139

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 003115 Figure 3-72. Flywheel Sensor (MPU1) NOTE: Reference Section 2.1 – General Troubleshooting Guidelines for proper procedures on testing connector plugs and incoming wires. NOTE: The flywheel sensor serves as the rpm sensor and the crank sensor for ignition. Tools Required • 0G41800SRV Breakout Harness • 10000029039 D2.2L Magnetic Pickup Adapter Procedure 1. Disconnect the flywheel sensor (MPU1) from the engine harness. 2. Set the DMM to measure resistance (Ω). 3. Connect one meter test lead to Wire 79 and the other meter test lead to wire 0 on MPU1. Measure and record the resistance. • See Table 3-6. If the flywheel sensor resistance is within limits, proceed to Step 4. • If the flywheel sensor resistance is not within limits, replace the flywheel sensor and refer to Section 4.1 Crank and Flywheel Sensor Installation and Adjustments (All Engines). Test 98 – Check Wires 79 and 0 General Theory Wire 79 sends a signal from the crankshaft sensor to the controller. If the controller doesn't receive the signal it will not move forward in the operation. Procedure 1. Locate and disconnect J3 connector at the Evolution Controller. 2. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 3. Connect one meter test lead to J3-10 (Wire 79) and J3-11 (Wire 0). Measure and record the resistance. Results 1. See Table 3-8. If DMM indicated a resistance within limits, replace controller. 2. If the DMM did not indicate a resistance value within limits, repair or replace Wire 79 and Wire 0 between the appropriate connector at the controller and the flywheel sensor. 140 Diagnostic Repair Manual

Table 3-8. Wires 79 and 0 Resistance Generator Resistance All (except D2.2L) 700–1100 ohms D2.2L 1500 ohms Test 101 – Check for Short Circuits General Theory If any fuse has opened, the most likely cause is a short to ground in the circuit that the fuse is protecting. Troubleshooting an open requires an understanding of the resistance differences between INFINITY and CONTINUITY. Figure 3-73 shows the DMM in two different states. The left DMM indicates an OPEN circuit or INFINITY. The right DMM indicates CONTINUITY. Since the resistance is very low it can be considered that 0.03 ohms equals a direct short, or a short to ground. A short to ground will usually cause a fuse to open. 002397 Figure 3-73. Infinity vs. Continuity In order to troubleshoot a circuit that has a short to ground the various legs and components of the circuit will need to be isolated. For example, if a circuit that includes a fuel solenoid has an open fuse in it, the cause could be the fuel solenoid itself or the positive power source wire. Begin troubleshooting by checking the resistance across the coil and the resistance from the coil to a clean frame ground. The resistance on the coil can be found in Table 3-9. NOTE: When measuring resistance the component must be completely isolated. Table 3-9. Coil Resistances (± 5%) Component Resistance Starter contactor 4.6 Ω Main fuel solenoid 15 Ω Cold start fuel solenoid 6.7 Ω Oxygen sensor heater 5.4 Ω Air/fuel solenoid 27 Ω Transfer relay 110 Ω Diagnostic Repair Manual Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests The coil should read INFINITY to ground. If it reads CONTINUITY to ground the problem has been located. If the coil tests good, test the positive power source wire for continuity to ground. Remove one end of the wire and place a meter lead on it, and place the other meter lead on a clean frame ground. The meter should read open if the wire is isolated, or the coil resistance if the component is still connected. If very low resistance is present the wire is shorted to ground. Locate the short and repair or replace the wire. Test 105 – Test Low Fuel Pressure Switch General Theory The low fuel pressure switch is a normally OPEN switch that will CLOSE when pressure is above 5 inches of water column. Wires 601 and 0 are connected to the switch. The controller will monitor Wire 601 for a ground, indicating the unit has 5 inches of water column or greater. When the switch is OPEN, 0.2 VDC will be present on Wire 601 indicating a low fuel pressure condition has occurred. This fault will not shutdown the engine. It will only indicate that there is an issue with fuel. Procedure 1. Remove Wire 601 and Wire 0 from the switch. 2. Turn off the fuel supply to the generator. 3. Set a DMM to measure resistance (Ω). 4. Connect one meter test lead to one terminal of the switch and the other meter test lead to the other terminal on the switch where Wires 601 and 0 were removed. INFINITY should be measured. 5. Turn on the fuel supply to the generator. 6. Repeat step 4, however this time CONTINUITY should be measured. 7. Set the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to AUTO. 8. Set a DMM to measure DC voltage. NOTE: Wires 601 and 0 should still be removed. 9. Connect one meter test lead to wire 601 and connect the other meter test to a clean frame ground. 0.2 VDC should be measured. 10. Set a DMM to measure resistance (Ω). 11. Connect one meter test lead to wire 0 and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. CONTINUITY should be measured. 12. If 0.2 VDC was measured in step 9, proceed to the results. If 0.2 VDC was not measured, proceed to step 13. 13. Disconnect the appropriate connector from the controller. 14. Set a DMM to measure resistance (Ω). NOTE: Reference Section 2.1 General Troubleshooting Guidelines for proper procedures on testing connector plugs and incoming wires. 141

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests 15. Connect one meter test lead to wire 601 that was removed from the switch and connect the other meter test lead to Wire 601. CONTINUITY should be measured. Results 1. If Steps 4, 5, 9, and 11 tested good, check for bad crimps on connectors or possibly a switch that has gone out of calibration in which case the switch would need to be replaced. 2. If either Steps 4 or 5 failed, replace the switch. 3. If Steps 4 and 5 tested good, but no voltage was measured in Step 12, and Step 15 was good, replace controller. 4. If Steps 4 and 5 tested good, but no voltage was measured in Step 12, and Step 15 tested bad, repair or replace Wire 601 between the controller and the low fuel pressure switch. Test 106 – Check Voltage on Wire 15B at the Ignition Module (If equipped) Procedure 1. Locate the ignition module mounted on the left hand side of the connection box. 2. Disconnect the J1 connector from the ignition module. 3. Set a DMM to measure DC voltage. 4. Connect one meter test lead to wire 15B and the other meter test lead to a clean frame ground. Measure and record the voltage indicated. 5. Connect one meter test lead to wire 0 and the other meter test lead to the positive post on the battery. Measure and record the voltage indicated. Results 1. If the DMM indicated battery voltage in Step 4 and Step 5, refer to the flow chart. 2. If the DMM indicated battery voltage in Step 4 and did not in Step 5, repair or replace Wire 0 between the ignition module and the battery. 3. If the DMM indicated battery voltage in Step 5 and did not in Step 4, repair or replace Wire 15B between the ignition module and the battery. Test 106A – Test the CAN bus Procedure 1. Identify Wire 744 (Can Bus Low) and Wire 743 (CAN Bus High) on the Evolution controller connector. With the connector still connected to the control panel and the system active, measure for DC voltage at Wire 744 and Wire 743 to ground. Record the measured voltages. 2. If Wire 744 measures approximately 1.67 VDC to ground and Wire 743 measures approximately 142 2.57 VDC to ground then verify DC voltage is present at Wire 15B for an ICM, Wire 172 for an ECM on a 4.5L engine, or Wire 14B on an ECG (Battery +). Verify Wire 0 has continuity to ground. If battery voltage and ground are present then replace the ICM, ECM, or ECG. 3. If Wire 744 measures approximately 1.88 VDC to ground and Wire 743 measures approximately 3.315 VDC to ground then verify continuity in Wire 744 and Wire 743 from the controller to the ICM, ECM, or ECG (verify male and female pins are making connection). 4. If approximately 0 volts are measured then disconnect the harness from the control panel and measure Pins 744 to 743. If 120 ohms is not measured then replace controller. 5. Before replacing the ICM, ECM, or ECG., disconnect all harnesses and measure at the ICM Pins 744 to 743. A resistance of approximately 120 Ohms should be present. Results 1. 120 Ohms should be measured between Wire 744 and Wire 743 on the Evolution controller, the ICM, ECM, or ECG. Wiring harness needs to be removed from the module during testing. If 120 ohms is not measured, replace the component. 2. 60 Ohms should be measured between Wire 744 and Wire 743 when the harness is plugged into the Evolution controller and the ICM, ECM, or ECG. Both modules must be powered down. If 120 Ohms is measured, repair Wire 744 or Wire 743. Test 108 – Test Ignition Coil General Theory Different engines will use different ignition coils. It is required to identify the correct procedure for the engine being worked on. These engine systems use an individual coil for each cylinder. For these types of systems, it is required to identify which coil needs to be tested using the ignition fault code. 1.5L and 2.4L (Individual Coil) Procedure NOTE: Ignition fault codes will identify which cylinder is faulty. 1. Locate the appropriate cylinder that is faulty. 2. Disconnect the coil connector. 3. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 4. Connect the meter test leads across the terminals exposed by disconnecting the coil. Measure and record the resistance. Results 1. If the DMM indicated approximately 1.6 ohms of resistance, refer to the flow chart. Diagnostic Repair Manual

2. If the DMM indicated INFINITY, high, or low resistance, replace ignition coil and retest. 1.6L (Coil Pack) Procedure 1. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 2. Connect one meter test lead to CP-2 (Wire 25B) and the other meter test lead to CP-3 (Wire 15A). Measure and record the resistance. 3. Connect one meter test lead to CP-1 (Wire 25A) and the other meter test lead to CP-3 (Wire 15A). Measure and record the resistance. Figure 3-74. 1.6L Coil Pack 005414 Results 1. If the DMM indicated approximately 0.9 ohms of resistance in Steps 2 and 3, refer back to the flow chart. 2. If the DMM indicated INFINITY, high or low resistance in either Step 2 or 3, replace the coil pack. 4.2L (Individual Coil) Procedure 1. Locate the appropriate cylinder that is faulty. 2. Disconnect the coil connector. 3. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 4. Connect the meter test leads across the terminals exposed by disconnecting the coil. Measure and record the resistance. Results 1. If the DMM indicated approximately 1 ohm of resistance, refer to the flow chart. 2. If the DMM indicated INFINITY, high, or low resistance, replace ignition coil and retest. 4.5L Procedure 1. Disconnect the electrical connection and the primary wire from the coil. 2. Set DMM to measure resistance. Primary resistance (measure 14E and 451–454) 1 ohm Secondary resistance (451–454 measure to any coil terminal) 9k ohms Diagnostic Repair Manual Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests Results 1. If Primary resistance is 1ohm and secondary resistance is 9K ohms, the coil is good, return to the flowchart. 2. If correct resistance is not measured, replace the faulty coil. 4.6L, 6.8L (Individual Coil) Procedure 1. Locate the appropriate cylinder that is faulty. 2. Disconnect the coil connector. 3. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 4. Connect the meter test leads across the terminals exposed by disconnecting the coil. Measure and record the resistance. Results 1. If the DMM indicated approximately 0.3–0.8 ohms of resistance, refer to the flow chart. 2. If the DMM indicated INFINITY, high, or low resistance, replace ignition coil and retest. Test 109 – Test Ignition Coil Wiring General Theory Different engines will use different ignition coils. It is necessary to identify the correct procedure for the engine being worked on. An individual coil is used for each cylinder. An ignition fault code is required to identify which coil wiring to test. See Figure 3-75 to identify test points for given coil number. Test 113—Test Air/Fuel Solenoid General Theory The air fuel ratio solenoid (AFS) is an electrically operated solenoid. The AFS controls the pressure on the regulator(s) diaphragm. The AFS is controlled by the airfuel ratio controller through Wire 808, which is normally open from the ground. The solenoid is powered by Wire 15A. When the solenoid is off (closed), atmospheric pressure is present on the face of the regulator's diaphragm. This produces a high output pressure from the regulator and results in rich operation of the engine. When the air-fuel ratio controller grounds Wire 808 the solenoid will energize. This allows negative pressure from the mixer to bias the regulator diaphragm face, which reduces the output pressure from the regulator and results in leaner operation of the engine. Procedure 1. Locate the AFS on the fuel regulator. 2. Set the generator to MANUAL mode. 3. Place a hand on the AFS to feel for pulsations. a. If the solenoid is pulsating, and the solenoid is working correctly, replace the Evolution Controller. b. If the solenoid is not pulsating, proceed to Step 4. NOTE: The pulsating rate varies between 1 to 10 times per second on differing units. To observe the pulse rate of the AFS set a DMM to measure frequency and measure between Wire 15A and Wire 808. 4. Locate and disconnect the J1 and J2 connectors from the back of the controller. 5. Set a DMM to measure resistance. 6. Connect one meter lead to Wire 808 and the other meter lead to Wire 15A. Measure a record the resistance. 7. Disconnect the AFS solenoid from wiring harness. 8. Set the DMM to measure resistance. 9. Connect meter leads across the terminals of the AFS solenoid. Measure and record the resistance. Results 1. If the DMM indicated approximately 27 ohms in Step 6, Replace the Evolution controller. 149

Test 114 – Coolant Sensor Circuit General Theory – Units without ECM The Evolution controller monitors the coolant sensor circuit for overheating. The coolant sensor is located near the thermostat and has one supply wire and one ground wire. The controller supplies a 3.3 VDC sensing voltage to the coolant sensor and monitors the changes in resistance based on the temperature of the engine. As the engine temperature goes up the resistance of the sensor goes down, pulling the supply voltage of the controller down. When the voltage reaches a predetermined level the High Temperature Alarm (ECode 1400) is triggered. The engine begins overheating at approximately 246 ºF (119 °C) with a resistance value of 102 ohms (±2.6%) and 2.17 VDC at the controller. Procedure – Units without ECM 1. Verify proper operation of the coolant sensor circuit by back probing between Wire 68 and Wire 0 at the controller to monitor voltage. As the engine warms up, use an external temperature measuring device, such as an infrared temperature gun, to monitor the engine temperature near the coolant sensor. (See Step 2 Note to activate the ECM.) a. 4.5–5.0 VDC should be measured. Results 1. If Wire 820G is not grounded, test and inspect the wiring harness for a break. Inspect the ECM plug for damaged pins. 2. If Wire 820A does not have any voltage when the ECM is active, test and inspect the wiring harness for a break. Inspect the ECM plug for damaged pins. 3. If no or low voltage is measured on Wire 752 or Wire 754, remove and inspect the sensor. The TMAP should produce between 2.4–2.6 VDC with the sensor removed from the system, but still plugged into the wire harness. Test and inspect the wiring harness for a break. Inspect the ECM plug for damaged pins. 152 Diagnostic Repair Manual

4. If Wire 820G is grounded correctly, Wire 820A has correct voltage, and no issues were found with Wires 752 and 754, replace the sensor. Test 122 – Fuel Pressure Sensor (FPS) General Theory The fuel pressure sensor is a 3-wire sensor. The sensor has a dedicated ground (Wire 820G), a dedicated power supply (Wire 820B, 4.5–5.0 VDC), and an output (Wire 797). 019836 Figure 3-91. Fuel Pressure Sensor (FPS) Procedure 1. Use needle-type back probes to verify Wire 820G is grounded to the main ground point on the engine. NOTE: This is where the negative battery cable is bolted to the side of the engine block. 2. Test Wire 820A to ground while the ECM is active. • 4.5–5.0 VDC should be measured. NOTE: To make the ECM active, access the Dealer Menu using Level 2 access code, and go to ECM firmware update, this will activate the ECM for a few seconds. 3. Test Wire 797 to ground for output voltage when the ECM is active. (See Step 2 Note to activate the ECM.) • Correct voltage output will range from 0.5–4.5VDC. Results 1. If Wire 820G is not grounded, test and inspect the wiring harness for a break. Inspect the ECM plug for damaged pins. 2. If Wire 820A does not have any voltage when the ECM is active, test and inspect the wiring harness for a break. Inspect the ECM plug for damaged pins. 3. If Wire 797 has low or no voltage when the ECM is active, test and inspect the wiring harness for a break. Inspect the ECM plug for damaged pins. • With the sensor removed from the system but plugged into the harness, the sensor should produce about 1.3 VDC. 4. If Wire 820G is grounded properly, Wire 820A has correct voltage, and no issues were found with Wire 797, replace the sensor. Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests Test 125 – Mixer Control Valve Assembly (TPS/EMC) General Theory The electronic mixer control (EMC) is positioned on the inlet of the fuel mixer. The EMC receives fuel from two fuel valves located on the frame rail. Fuel inlet pressure to the EMC is 3.5–14 in W.C. The EMC controls fuel flow to the engine to maintain performance and emissions characteristics. The valve is controlled by a two-coil stepper motor. NOTE: The EMC and TPS are components of a single assembly. If either component is determined to be faulty the mixer assembly must be replaced in its entirety. Test 128 – Electronic Throttle Control Valve (ETC) General Theory The electronic throttle control valve (ETC) is a motorcontrolled throttle valve with a built-in throttle position feedback sensor. A 5-wire harness connects the ETC to the ECM for throttle control and throttle position feedback. 019832 Figure 3-93. Electronic Throttle Control Valve (ETC) Procedure 1 – Test Power to ETC 1. Set DMM to measure DC voltage. 2. Measure Wire 770 (12 VDC) to Wire 771 (negative). a. If 12 VDC is measured, the power circuit is good. Continue to Procedure 2 – Test the Feedback Circuit. b. If no or low voltage is measured continue to Step 3. 3. Set DMM to DC voltage. 4. Measure Wires 770 and 771 at the ECM. a. If 12 VDC is now measured, repair wiring between the ECM and the ETC. b. If no voltage is measured, visually inspect the ECM connector and pins. If no other issues found, replace the ECM. Procedure 2 – Test the Feedback Circuit 1. Set DMM to measure DC voltage. 2. Measure Wire 820B to ground. If 4.5–5.0 VDC is measured, continue to Step 4. If no or low voltage is measured continue to Step 3 3. Measure DC voltage on Wire 820B at the ECM. a. If proper voltage is now measured, repair the wiring between the ECM and the ETC. 4. Set DMM to measure resistance. 5. Measure Wire 820G to the ground block. a. If low resistance is measured, continue to the next step. b. If resistance is high or INFINITE, repair Wire 820G. 6. Measure Wire 776 at the mixer connection to ground. a. Back probe Wire 766 with positive meter lead. b. Place the negative meter lead to a good ground or battery negative. (1) If 0.5–4.5 VDC is measured, continue to Step 7. (2) If no or low voltage is measured, Wire 820B and Wire 820G are good, replace the ETC valve. 7. Measure Wire 776 at the ECM connection to ground. a. Back probe Wire 766 with positive meter lead. b. Place the negative meter lead to a good ground or battery negative. (1) If no or low voltage is measured, repair the Wire 766. (2) If voltage is measured, inspect the ECM plug and pins. If all is good and problem still exists, replace the ECM. Results 1. If no voltage is measured on Wire 820B at the ECM, replace the ECM. 2. If no or low voltage is measured on Wire 766 at the ETC, replace the ETC. 154 Diagnostic Repair Manual

Test 129 – Test Fuel Solenoids General Theory If equipped with Generac 4.5L engine, there are two fuel solenoids located on the fuel rail. One solenoid is controlled by the Evolution Controller and the other is controlled by the ECM. This way, either controller can have a fatal alarm and turn off the generator. Figure 3-94. Fuel Solenoids 019830 Procedure 1. Connect a manometer to the Pete's plug located on the fuel rail before the two solenoids. 2. Press the MANUAL button to initiate a start. A normal reading of 3.5–14 in H2O should be measured. a. If correct fuel pressure was measured, proceed to Step 3. b. If no fuel pressure was measured, proceed to Test 58. 3. Locate FS1(Fuel Solenoid 1). Test wire 14A to Wire 610 for DC voltage at the solenoid plug. a. Place the generator in MANUAL mode. b. If battery voltage was measured, suspect a faulty fuel solenoid. c. If no voltage is measured, repeat Step 3 and measure from Wire 14A to a good clean ground. (1) If voltage is now measured, continue to Step 4. (2) If no voltage is measured, continue to Step 5. 4. At the same plug, locate Wire 610. This is a ground provided from the ECM. Measure for DC voltage from Wire 610 to ground. a. Place the generator in MANUAL mode. b. If no voltage is measured, set the DMM to measure continuity and verify Wire 610 has continuity between the solenoid and the ECM. Diagnostic Repair Manual Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests c. Repair as necessary. 5. Locate Fuel Solenoid 2 (FS2). Test Wire 14A to ground for DC voltage at the solenoid plug. a. If battery voltage was measured, continue to Step 6 b. If no voltage is measured, go to Step 7. 6. At the same plug, set DMM to measure continuity. a. Verify that Wire 0 has continuity to the ground bar. b. Repair if necessary. 7. Test Wire 14A from the solenoid to the Evolution controller a. Set DMM to measure DC voltage. b. Using the proper back probes, place the black meter lead on a good ground and leave it there for the remainder of this test. c. Place the red meter lead on Wire 14A at the FSR plug. d. Place the generator in MANUAL mode. (1) If no voltage is measured, continue to next step. (2) If battery voltage is now measured, repair Wire 14A between the solenoid and FSR plug. e. Back-probe the red meter lead on COP2 Pin 1. (1) Place the generator in MANUAL mode. (2) If no voltage is measured, continue to next step. (3) If battery voltage is now measured, repair Wire 14A between the FSR plug and COP2 Pin 1. f. Locate the J1 Molex connector on the back of the Evolution controller. Back probe the position where Wire 14A is located. (1) Place the generator in MANUAL mode. (2) If no voltage is measured, continue to next step. (3) If battery voltage is now measured, repair Wire 14A between the COR2 and J1 Molex connector. g. Verify the controller is commanding on the output for fuel. If battery voltage is not being supplied to the pin on the back of the controller where Wire 14A is placed, replace the controller. Results 1. If battery voltage is present at Wire 14a and Wire 610 for FS1 and the solenoid is not opening, replace FS1. 2. If battery voltage is present at Wires 14A and 0 for FS2 and the solenoid is not opening, replace FS2. 3. If battery voltage is not present, use procedure above to determine cause of problem. 155

Section 3.5 DC Diagnostic Tests Test 130 – Ignition Relay (IR) General Theory The ignition relay (IR) is located in the compartment above the Evolution controller and above the run relay. The IR receives power for the coil and for the output from Wire 13. The relay is controlled by Wire 608 which is connected to the ECM. This a control ground so that when the ECM needs this relay to become active, the ECM will pull Wire 608 low, energizing the relay. The IR provides power for the ignition coils, the oxygen sensor heater, and the CAC bypass solenoid. Procedure 1. Test Wire 13 to ground. Wire 13 goes to two places on the relay, the coil and the common. Test for DC voltage in both locations. a. If battery voltage is measured, continue to the next step. b. If battery voltage is not measured, go to results. 2. Test Wire 608 to ground. Test resistance from wire 608 on the coil of the relay to ground. a. If resistance is low continue to the next step. b. If resistance is very high or open, go to results. IMPORTANT NOTE: The ECM must be activated in order to test Wire 608 to ground. This can be done by going to “EDIT” and reading the engine run hours. For this information to be displayed, the ECM will be activated by the generator's controller. 3. Test Wire 14D to ground. Test for DC battery voltage. a. If battery voltage is measured, continue to the next step. b. If no or low voltage is measured, go to results. 4. Test F4 fuse, replace if faulty. Results 1. If Wire 13 has no or low battery voltage at the relay, test the harness back toward the battery looking for a break in the wire. 2. If an open or high resistance is measured on Wire 608, test the harness back to the ECM. Check the ECM plug for a faulty pin. 3. If no or low voltage is measured on 14D, and Wire 13 and Wire 608 test good, replace the relay. Section 4.1 Generator Adjustments Calibrate Voltage Regulator Discussion When voltage output is too high, it is possible to adjust voltage output of the generator. To access this menu a password will be required to be entered into controller. Anytime a new generator is installed, or an Evolution Controller is replaced, it is necessary to calibrate the voltage output of the generator. Procedure 1. Set a digital multimeter (DMM) to measure AC voltage. 2. Set up the DMM to measure output voltage on the breaker. NOTE: Measure voltage at the input side of the breaker. 3. Open the main line circuit breaker (MLCB) on the generator. 4. Refer to the programing section for the specific panel being used. Use the voltage adjust for Evolution panel or the calibration for the Nexus panel to set the units voltage. 5. Set AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch to MANUAL. IMPORTANT NOTE: The engine will crank and possibly start when the AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch is set to MANUAL. CAUTION Equipment damage. Do not adust calibration factor below 990 or above 1040. Doing so could result in equipment damage. (000326) 6. While the unit is running, use the up or down arrow buttons to adjust the calibration setting. A higher value will create a lower voltage at the breaker and vice versa a lower value will create a higher voltage at the breaker. 7. Once a desired output voltage has been achieved, press ENTER to save the new setting. NOTE: The calibration setting will reset to being a password protected option after the controller is left idle. Verification While the unit is running, verify that the output voltage at the breaker is consistent within 5 volts to what the controller displays in the Dealer Display Menu under Outputs. Results 1. If during the verification process the output voltage at the breaker and the display match and the calibration setting was not adjusted outside of the window, the calibration was successful. 2. AUX Shutdown New specifications in Article 445.18(B) of the 2017 National Electrical Code (NEC) require generators to be equipped with an independent means of shutting down the prime mover (engine). The shutdown mechanism, when activated, requires a mechanical reset. Generators 15 kW and larger require two engine shutdown switches. NOTE: Some Authorities Having Jurisdiction (AHJs) and local codes require Protector diesel generators to be equipped with an optional Emergency Stop Switch (Estop). The E-stop is offered separately from this kit as model G0065100. Firmware Update (if required) The generator controller may require a firmware update. Firmware version 1.19 or later is required. Section 4.1 Generator Adjustments Verify controller firmware version. If an update is required, install latest version before testing engine shutdown switches. 1. Connect negative battery terminal and tighten nut. 2. Install 7.5 A fuse and configure install wizard. 3. With generator controller OFF, enter Edit menu. 4. Scroll through the options and select “Update Firmware.” Press Enter. 5. Insert a USB drive with current firmware into controller port. Follow prompts. 6. After firmware has been updated, press “Escape” until sub menu screen displays. 7. Enter dealer menu. 8. Select “Dealer/Edit” menu. 9. Scroll through the options and select “Auxiliary Stop Setting.” 10. Select “Auxiliary Shutdown.” 11. Press Escape until submenu screen displays. Activate Engine Shutdown Functionality Verify firmware version of the controller is correct as specified in Firmware Update (if required) . If an update is required, download and install the latest firmware before proceeding. The controller must detect the installed switches to activate the engine shutdown functionality. 1. Verify controller is powered and generator is OFF. 2. Turn rocker switches ON to verify switches are disengaged. 3. Turn one rocker switch OFF. The controller should detect that the switch has been engaged and will display “Auxiliary Shutdown.” • If alarm appears on controller screen, turn rocker switch ON and clear alarm. • If alarm does not appear on controller screen, engine shutdown switch is not functioning. Verify firmware version meets requirements. Disconnect power and re-check wiring installation. Contact Generac Technical Support if the problem cannot be identified or if you need assistance. 4. Repeat steps 1–3 for second rocker switch. Test Switch Operation Test engine shutdown switches after installation to verify proper operation. 1. Verify rocker switches are ON. 2. Press MANUAL key on control panel keypad to start engine. 3. With engine running, press one of the engine shutdown switches to OFF. Engine should shut down immediately. • If engine stops, press engine shutdown switch to ON, clear alarm on controller, and restart engine to 164 verify generator is operating normally. After verifying normal operation of first switch, verify operation of second switch. • If engine does not stop, engine shutdown switch is not functioning correctly. Stop generator through the control panel, and re-check wiring installation. Contact Generac Technical Support if the problem cannot be identified or if you need assistance. 4. Show homeowner how to operate engine shutdown switches. Remind him or her that the engine shutdown switches are not intended to be the primary means to shut down the generator under normal operating conditions. Accidental activation of an engine shutdown switch will prevent the generator from operating during a power outage. Diagnostic Repair Manual

Replacement Procedure 1. Locate the unit data label and record the following information: • kW • Engine displacement (L) • Voltage Code The unit model code breakdown will provide the unit information. Unit Model code breakdown example: QT 02724A _ _ X The first three digits represent the kW rating: 027 = 27 kW The next two digits represent the engine displacement in liters: 24 = 2.4L The next letter identifies the voltage code of the unit: A = A code, 120/240 ~ A = 120/240, 1 Phase; G = 120/208, 3 Phase; J = 120/240, 3 Phase; K = 277/480, 3 Phase; M = 110/220, 1 Phase, 50 Hz. The last letter designates if it is a catalyst equipped unit. ~ X = Non-catalyst C = Catalyst. You will also need to know the fuel type the unit is using; it will be either NG (natural gas) or LP (liquid propane vapor). 2. Refer to the appropriate SIB (service information bulletin) and record the voltage code (V-Code) and parameter Group for the generator model the panel is installed on. You will need this information in steps 5–6 of the configuration procedure. V-Code = Parameter Group = NOTE: Make sure the panel AUTO-OFF-MANUAL switch is OFF when connecting and powering the panel. 3. After the replacement panel has been mounted, connected, and powered up, the panel display will ask you to set the time and the exerciser function. The panel will not need to be re-registered. CAUTION Equipment damage. Do not run unit until Nexus panel has been properly configured. Failure to do so could cause severe equipment damage. (000328) Refer to SIB14-02-ELIQ (Evolution). Use the information from the unit data label to find the corresponding V-code and parameter group number (to be entered into the appropriate fields in the control panel).
